items.body:
broken out from #13564 , which partially dupes #9147

>  JoinCondition._track_overlapping_sync_targets (_JoinCondition on main). It is a class-level WeakKeyDictionary that only exists for the "relationship X will copy column Q to column P, which conflicts with ..." warning. The keys (to_ columns) are weak, but the values are plain Column objects (from_). As soon as the from_ column can reach the to_ column through strong references, the weak key is kept alive by the dictionary's own value and the entry never expires. That happens for example when an Index built from an ORM attribute (Index("ix", Parent.id.desc())) is attached to the table: the expression is annotated with the mapper, so Table → mapper → registry → the other classes → the to_ column. In my case every rebuilt class left ~1000 Column objects, the mapper and the class behind, roughly 7–9 MB per rebuild per process.

```py
import gc, weakref
import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.orm import registry, relationship, configure_mappers, Mapper
try:
    from sqlalchemy.orm.relationships import JoinCondition
except ImportError:  # main
    from sqlalchemy.orm.relationships import _JoinCondition as JoinCondition


def build(orm_index=False, declare_last=False):
    reg = registry()
    Base = reg.generate_base()

    class Parent(Base):
        __tablename__ = "parent"
        id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
        if declare_last:
            @classmethod
            def __declare_last__(cls):
                pass

    class Child(Base):
        __tablename__ = "child"
        id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
        parent_id = sa.Column(sa.ForeignKey("parent.id"))
        parent = relationship(Parent)

    if orm_index:
        sa.Index("ix_parent_id_desc", Parent.id.desc())

    configure_mappers()
    refs = (weakref.ref(Parent), weakref.ref(Child), weakref.ref(Parent.__table__))
    reg.dispose()
    return refs


def listeners():
    return sum(len(c) for c in Mapper.dispatch.after_configured._clslevel.values())


print(sa.__version__)
for kwargs in ({}, {"orm_index": True}, {"declare_last": True}):
    alive = []
    for _ in range(5):
        refs = build(**kwargs)
        gc.collect(); gc.collect()
        alive.append(tuple(r() is not None for r in refs))
    print(kwargs, "Parent/Child/Table alive:", alive,
          "| sync_targets:", len(JoinCondition._track_overlapping_sync_targets),
          "| after_configured listeners:", listeners())
    if kwargs.get("orm_index"):
        JoinCondition._track_overlapping_sync_targets.clear(); gc.collect()
        print("   after clearing _track_overlapping_sync_targets -> Parent alive:", refs[0]() is not None)
```

items.title: Disposed declarative classes are kept alive by _track_overlapping_sync_targets and by the __declare_last__ "after_configured" listener

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: declarative
labels.description: has to do with the declarative API, scanning classes and mixins for attributes to be mapped

labels.name: memory
labels.description: issues related to memory use

items.body:
### Describe the bug

I rebuild ORM classes at runtime (tenant-defined tables, so a class gets re-created when its schema changes) and noticed the process grows by several MB every time, even though the old registry/mappers are disposed and nothing of mine references the old classes any more. Tracking it down with `gc.get_referrers` ended in two places inside SQLAlchemy that hold on to mapped classes for the whole process lifetime:

1. **`JoinCondition._track_overlapping_sync_targets`** (`_JoinCondition` on main). It is a class-level `WeakKeyDictionary` that only exists for the "relationship X will copy column Q to column P, which conflicts with ..." warning. The keys (`to_` columns) are weak, but the values are plain `Column` objects (`from_`). As soon as the `from_` column can reach the `to_` column through strong references, the weak key is kept alive by the dictionary's own value and the entry never expires. That happens for example when an `Index` built from an ORM attribute (`Index("ix", Parent.id.desc())`) is attached to the table: the expression is annotated with the mapper, so Table → mapper → registry → the other classes → the `to_` column. In my case every rebuilt class left ~1000 `Column` objects, the mapper and the class behind, roughly 7–9 MB per rebuild per process.

2. **`__declare_last__` / `__declare_first__`**. `_ClassScanMapperConfig._setup_declared_events()` registers a closure on `Mapper` `"after_configured"` for every class that defines the hook. The closure holds the config object (and through it the class), it is never removed — `registry.dispose()` doesn't know about it — and the listener list on `Mapper` grows by one per class ever mapped and is run on every `configure_mappers()`.

Reproduced on 1.4.54, 2.0.52 and current main.

### To Reproduce

```python
import gc, weakref
import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.orm import registry, relationship, configure_mappers, Mapper
try:
    from sqlalchemy.orm.relationships import JoinCondition
except ImportError:  # main
    from sqlalchemy.orm.relationships import _JoinCondition as JoinCondition


def build(orm_index=False, declare_last=False):
    reg = registry()
    Base = reg.generate_base()

    class Parent(Base):
        __tablename__ = "parent"
        id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
        if declare_last:
            @classmethod
            def __declare_last__(cls):
                pass

    class Child(Base):
        __tablename__ = "child"
        id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
        parent_id = sa.Column(sa.ForeignKey("parent.id"))
        parent = relationship(Parent)

    if orm_index:
        sa.Index("ix_parent_id_desc", Parent.id.desc())

    configure_mappers()
    refs = (weakref.ref(Parent), weakref.ref(Child), weakref.ref(Parent.__table__))
    reg.dispose()
    return refs


def listeners():
    return sum(len(c) for c in Mapper.dispatch.after_configured._clslevel.values())


print(sa.__version__)
for kwargs in ({}, {"orm_index": True}, {"declare_last": True}):
    alive = []
    for _ in range(5):
        refs = build(**kwargs)
        gc.collect(); gc.collect()
        alive.append(tuple(r() is not None for r in refs))
    print(kwargs, "Parent/Child/Table alive:", alive,
          "| sync_targets:", len(JoinCondition._track_overlapping_sync_targets),
          "| after_configured listeners:", listeners())
    if kwargs.get("orm_index"):
        JoinCondition._track_overlapping_sync_targets.clear(); gc.collect()
        print("   after clearing _track_overlapping_sync_targets -> Parent alive:", refs[0]() is not None)
```

### Error

Output is the same on 1.4.54, 2.0.52 and main:

```
{}                      Parent/Child/Table alive: [(False, False, False), ...]  | sync_targets: 0 | after_configured listeners: 0
{'orm_index': True}     Parent/Child/Table alive: [(True, True, True), ...]     | sync_targets: 5 | after_configured listeners: 0
   after clearing _track_overlapping_sync_targets -> Parent alive: False
{'declare_last': True}  Parent/Child/Table alive: [(True, False, True), ...]    | sync_targets: 5 | after_configured listeners: 5
```

Expected: after `registry.dispose()` (and dropping my own references) the classes, mappers and tables are collectable, and nothing on the `Mapper` class grows with the number of registries ever created.

### Versions

- OS: Linux
- Python: 3.10 / 3.11
- SQLAlchemy: 1.4.54, 2.0.52, main
- Database: PostgreSQL (not needed for the reproducer)
- DBAPI: psycopg2

### Additional context

I have a patch that makes both structures hold the class/column weakly and removes the declared-events listeners when the class is unmapped (`registry._dispose_manager_and_mapper`); the reproducer above prints all `False` with it and the ORM test suites I ran still pass. I'll open a PR referencing this issue.

For anyone hitting this before a release: clearing the mapper's entries from `_track_overlapping_sync_targets` and removing the `after_configured` listener whose closure holds the class, at the point where the class is disposed, works around it.

### Describe the bug

The behaviour of calling `.one()` on an AppenderQuery differs on whether the instance is in the session or not when using SQLAlchemy 1.4 and 2.0, but not 1.3. When the instance is not in the session, I expect a result or a `NoResultFound` exception as I get in 1.3, but in 1.4 and 2.0 I instead get a `TypeError: 'OrderedIdentitySet' object is not an iterator`.

### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected

_No response_

### SQLAlchemy Version in Use

1.4.52, 2.0.31

### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)

pysqlite, pymysql

### Database Vendor and Major Version

SQLite, MySQL 8

### Python Version

3.8.18

### Operating system

OSX

### To Reproduce

```python
from sqlalchemy import *
from sqlalchemy.orm import *
try:
    from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base
except ImportError:
    from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base

Session = sessionmaker()
engine = create_engine("sqlite:///:memory:")
Base = declarative_base()


class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "user"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)


class Address(Base):
    __tablename__ = "address"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    user_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey("user.id"), nullable=False)

    user = relationship(User, backref=backref("addresses", lazy="dynamic"))


connection = engine.connect()
with connection.begin():
    Base.metadata.create_all(connection)
session = Session(bind=connection)
user = User()
#session.add(user)
user.addresses.one()
```


### Error

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "minimal.py", line 34, in <module>
    user.addresses.one()
  File ".../lib/python3.8/site-packages/sqlalchemy/orm/query.py", line 2778, in one
    return self._iter().one()  # type: ignore
  File ".../lib/python3.8/site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/result.py", line 1810, in one
    return self._only_one_row(
  File ".../lib/python3.8/site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/result.py", line 749, in _only_one_row
    row: Optional[_InterimRowType[Any]] = onerow(hard_close=True)
  File ".../lib/python3.8/site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/result.py", line 1673, in _fetchone_impl
    return self._real_result._fetchone_impl(hard_close=hard_close)
  File ".../lib/python3.8/site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/result.py", line 2259, in _fetchone_impl
    row = next(self.iterator, _NO_ROW)
TypeError: 'OrderedIdentitySet' object is not an iterator
``` 

### Additional context

I'm seeing this error as part of an in-progress migration from 1.4 to 2.0, where the existing application tests occasionally  
calls `.one()` on `AppenderQuery` to perform assertions on instances that are known to be present.

The actual code path that triggers this looks something like this:
```
# Test code
user = User()
session.add(user)
session.flush()
# Application code
session.rollback()  # an application exception causes a rollback
# Test code
user.addresses.one()   # expecting a NoResultFound error
```
In the application code, if no exception is thrown, a `session.commit()` is executed instead of a  `session.rollback()`, and the behaviour is again as expected: `NoResultFound` (or if there actually is a result, then the result is returned).

Behaviour for the various SQLAlchemy versions I have been using:
```
        in session     not in session
SA13:  NoResultFound    NoResultFound
SA14:  NoResultFound    TypeError
SA20:  NoResultFound    TypeError
```

Thanks for a fantastic library.

items.body:
**Describe the bug**

By default, different PostgreSQL drivers may return different Python types for JSON(B) values. For example of the same JSON dict, psycopg2 returns `dict` while asyncpg returns `str`. SQLAlchemy should eliminate the difference and return consistent results. The issue is, the asyncpg dialect/driver cannot parse JSON into dict if the SA type is unspecified (executing raw SQL for example), please see below.

**To Reproduce**

```py
import asyncio

import sqlalchemy as sa
from sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql import JSONB
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine


async def main():
    e = sa.create_engine("postgresql+psycopg2:///", future=True)
    ae = create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg:///")

    for json_type in [sa.JSON, JSONB]:
        print(json_type.__visit_name__)

        # create test tables
        metadata = sa.MetaData()
        users = sa.Table("users", metadata, sa.Column("profile", json_type))
        metadata.create_all(e)

        queries = [
            ("clause", sa.select([users.c.profile])),
            ("text  ", sa.text("SELECT profile FROM users")),
        ]

        with e.connect() as conn:
            conn.execute(users.insert().values(profile=dict(a=1, b=2)))
            for exec_type, obj in queries:
                print("sync ", exec_type, type(conn.scalar(obj)).__name__)
            conn.execute(users.delete())

        async with ae.connect() as conn:
            await conn.execute(users.insert().values(profile=dict(a=1, b=2)))
            for exec_type, obj in queries:
                print("async", exec_type, type(await conn.scalar(obj)).__name__)
            await conn.execute(users.delete())

        metadata.drop_all(e)


asyncio.run(main())
```

**Expected results**

```
JSON
sync  clause dict
sync  text   dict
async clause dict
async text   dict
JSONB
sync  clause dict
sync  text   dict
async clause dict
async text   dict
```

**Actual results**

```
JSON
sync  clause dict
sync  text   dict
async clause dict
async text   str
JSONB
sync  clause dict
sync  text   dict
async clause dict
async text   str
```

**Versions.**
 - OS: Darwin Kernel Version 19.5.0
 - Python: Python 3.8.2
 - SQLAlchemy: 1.4.0b1 @ 4d17fe4063adef50c1d529993e0b047f503940e2
 - Database: PostgreSQL 12.4
 - DBAPI: asyncpg 0.21.0, psycopg2 2.8.5 (dt dec pq3 ext lo64)

**Additional context**

I have 2 candidate solutions:

1. Override `NullType.result_processor()`. This is simpler but slightly hacky:

```patch
diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/asyncpg.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/asyncpg.py
index 780e23844..a62db1a5e 100644
--- a/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/asyncpg.py
+++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/asyncpg.py
@@ -70,6 +70,9 @@ try:
 except ImportError:
     _python_UUID = None

+JSON_COLTYPE = 114
+JSONB_COLTYPE = 3802
+

 class AsyncpgTime(sqltypes.Time):
     def get_dbapi_type(self, dbapi):
@@ -218,6 +221,15 @@ class AsyncpgOID(OID):
         return dbapi.INTEGER


+class AsyncpgNullType(sqltypes.NullType):
+    def result_processor(self, dialect, coltype):
+        if coltype == JSON_COLTYPE:
+            return json.JSON().result_processor(dialect, coltype)
+        if coltype == JSONB_COLTYPE:
+            return json.JSONB().result_processor(dialect, coltype)
+        return super().result_processor(dialect, coltype)
+
+
 class PGExecutionContext_asyncpg(PGExecutionContext):
     def pre_exec(self):
         if self.isddl:
@@ -720,6 +732,7 @@ class PGDialect_asyncpg(PGDialect):
             sqltypes.Enum: AsyncPgEnum,
             OID: AsyncpgOID,
             REGCLASS: AsyncpgREGCLASS,
+            sqltypes.NullType: AsyncpgNullType,
         },
     )

```

(This was the solution in GINO, see python-gino/gino#305, python-gino/gino#403)

2. Use asyncpg-native `set_type_codec()`. This is more consistent with psycopg2 impl but longer. Moreover, it revealed another issue, please see TODO below:

```patch

 import collections
 import decimal
 import itertools
+import json as json_lib
 import re

 from . import json
@@ -123,11 +124,17 @@ class AsyncpgJSON(json.JSON):

+    def result_processor(self, dialect, coltype):

+

@@ -500,6 +507,7 @@ class AsyncAdapt_asyncpg_connection:

         """

+        # TODO: this causes failure in future set_type_codec() below
         await self._connection.set_type_codec(
             "char",
             schema="pg_catalog",
@@ -508,6 +516,24 @@ class AsyncAdapt_asyncpg_connection:
             format="text",

+    def setup_json_handlers(self, serializer, deserializer):
+        self.await_(
+            self._connection.set_type_codec(
+                "json",
+                encoder=serializer,
+                decoder=deserializer,

@@ -796,5 +822,34 @@ class PGDialect_asyncpg(PGDialect):
                 e, self.dbapi.InterfaceError
             ) and "connection is closed" in str(e)

+    def on_connect(self):
+        fns = []
+        if self.isolation_level is not None:
+
+            def on_connect(conn):
```

items.body:
### Describe the bug

sqlite3.Connection.create_function
- py38>=: no longer supports kwarg, deterministic
- py38<, sqlite3.Connection.create_function requires kwarg, deterministic

[sqlite create_function docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.create_function)

> `[NotSupportedError](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.NotSupportedError) – If deterministic is used with SQLite versions **older than** 3.8.3.
> 

In [pysqlite.py](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/main/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/sqlite/pysqlite.py),

SQLiteDialect_pysqlite.on_connect, attempts to register two user-defined functions: regexp and floor.

Affects all python versions cuz the logic is reversed, kwargs deterministic:
-  is provided when it shouldn't
- is missing when it's needed



### Separate issue

The exact cutoff version is py383, but the code only handles py[major][minor], not py[major][minor][patch]. So that is dodgy and should be a separate issue. The suggested changes does not address that issue. One issue at a time


### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected

_No response_

### SQLAlchemy Version in Use

2.0.5.post1

### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)

sqlite+pysqlite, sqlite+pycipher

### Database Vendor and Major Version

sqlite3

### Python Version

3.9.16

### Operating system

Void Linux amd64

### To Reproduce


#### Affected code segment

```
        if util.py38 and self._get_server_version_info(None) >= (3, 9):
            # sqlite must be **greater than** 3.8.3 for deterministic=True
            # https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.create_function
            # the check is more conservative since there were still issues
            # with following 3.8 sqlite versions
            create_func_kw = {"deterministic": True}
        else:
            create_func_kw = {}
```

#### Suggested changes
```
        if util.py38 and self._get_server_version_info(None) >= (3, 9):
            create_func_kw = {}
        else:
            # sqlite must be **less than** 3.8.3 for deterministic=True
            # https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.create_function
            # the check is more conservative since there were still issues
            # with following 3.8 sqlite versions
            create_func_kw = {"deterministic": True}
```
Lets review the changed code to see if it follows the docs

> `[NotSupportedError](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.NotSupportedError) – If deterministic is used with SQLite versions **older than** 3.8.3.
> 

```if util.py38 and self._get_server_version_info(None) >= (3, 9)```

util.py38 means py38 and greater. So if py38+ would trigger NotSupportedError exception if kwarg deterministic is used. In the suggested code kwarg deterministic is not provided, ```create_func_kw = {}```

In the else condition, meaning prior to py38, kwarg deterministic is supported and should be provided ```create_func_kw = {"deterministic": True}```


### Error

Install sqlalchemy package into a virtual environment py39

Attempting to connect, using sqlalchemy2.0 Core connect(), to a sqlite+pysqlite or sqlite+pycipher database, irregardless persistent or in-memory, results in ```sqlalchemy.exc.DatabaseError```

items.title: transaction / execution simplification for 2.0

labels.name: engine
labels.description: engines, connections, transactions, isolation levels, execution options

labels.name: big job
labels.description: a major change that requires a lot of knowledge and work

labels.name: alchemy 2
labels.description: goes along with the 2.0 milestone to aid in searching

items.body:
in 2.0 we seek to completely simplify Core execution and transaction control and this will also impact the ORM.

The ideas area discussed at https://gist.github.com/zzzeek/dd590d0a3485b7f19cab0322c48ece36 .  Here is the theme:

   When SQLAlchemy was written, Python was at 2.3.   There were no context managers.  Now there are!  Everything is different.

So with this:

* all implicit execution is gone, e.g. statement.execute()
* all .bind is gone, e.g. see #4634 
* engine.execute() is gone

The only pattern is:

```
with engine.begin() as conn:
   conn.execute(...)
```

* Connection gains a `commit()` method so commit-as-you-go can happen in the block
* Connection gains a `rollback()` method which auto-begins in the block.

The above two methods CANNOT BE CALLED OUTSIDE OF THE BEGIN STATE.   That is, this will work very much like `Session` without autocommit.

* As part of this also, *all autocommit is gone*.   From ORM, from Core, take it right out.  It no longer applies since all transaction blocks are explicit.  this will remove an enormous amount of complexity and conceptual overhead for users learning,etc.

* we will need a vast number of documentation changes

* savepoints continue to work like they do now:

```
   with connection.begin() as conn:
        with conn.begin_savepoint():
            ....
```


What's not clear is if there is still an explicit `Transaction` object.    We may need to maintain this because in particular it's not clear we can just drop XA transactions as we see in #4608.    #4608 needs to be addressed as part of this issue.   I think we should likely keep XA mostly like it is after some consideration, but what's not clear is if we want it controlled from Connection or from a Transaction object.    I think the Transaction object itself might be overkill.

* more things I'm not thinking of at the moment

### Describe the bug

# Issue

When streaming objects from a large table like so:
```python
for user in session.query(User):
    pass
```
memory usage increases constantly. This true under cpython, but especially prominent under pypy where we can end up with 10s of gigabytes allocated for objects that are no longer referenced.

# Expected behaviour

I would expect the memory usage to be constant when streaming data like this.

### To Reproduce

```python
import gc
import os
import random
import sys
from csv import DictReader, DictWriter
from string import ascii_letters


try:
    import psutil
    from sqlalchemy import create_engine
    from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String
    from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
    from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
    from tqdm import tqdm
except ImportError:
    print("Please run 'pip install sqlalchemy psutil tqdm'")
    exit(1)


def printmem(msg):
    # Not crazy accurate, but good enough for our purposes
    raw = psutil.Process().memory_info().rss // (1024 * 1024)
    print(f"{msg} {raw}m")


def rstring():
    return "".join(random.sample(ascii_letters, 8))


# Setting up SQLA
Base = declarative_base()

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'user'
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String)
    fullname = Column(String)
    nickname = Column(String)


if not os.path.exists("user.csv"):
    if os.path.exists("db.sqlite"):
        os.remove("db.sqlite")

    print("Generating data - this may take some time.")
    with open("user.csv", "w") as f:
        writer = DictWriter(
            f, fieldnames=("id", "name", "fullname", "nickname")
        )
        writer.writeheader()
        for n in tqdm(range(10_000_000)):
            writer.writerow(dict(id=n, name=rstring(), fullname=rstring(), nickname=rstring()))


    # Bypass SQLA for the initial load (let's not skew our statistics)
    printmem("Before inserting")
    engine = create_engine('sqlite:///db.sqlite', echo=False)
    Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
    _con = engine.raw_connection()
    _cur = _con.cursor()

    with open("user.csv") as f:
        reader = DictReader(f)

        _cur.executemany(
            "INSERT INTO user (id, name, fullname, nickname) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?);",
            (
                (int(row["id"]), row["name"], row["fullname"], row["nickname"])
                for row in reader
            ),
        )

    _con.commit()
    _cur.close()
    _con.close()
    engine.dispose()
    gc.collect()
    printmem("After inserting")

# Fresh engine and time for the actual benchmark
engine = create_engine('sqlite:///db.sqlite', echo=False)
Session = sessionmaker(bind=engine)
Session = sessionmaker()
Session.configure(bind=engine)
session = Session()

try:
    N = int(sys.argv[1])
except IndexError:
    N = int(input("Enter number of rows to stream: (0-10000000)"))
for user in session.query(User).limit(N):
    assert user.name
    # session.commit()  # Makes no difference

printmem("After querying")
session.commit()
printmem("After commit")
gc.collect()
printmem("After gc collect\n")
```

items.body:
Running the example below in 1.3 would not configure the mapper when a select with `correlate_except` is used in a `column_property`. In 1.4 it's instead called. 
This causes issues while importing classes, since not all files may be imported before mapper configure is called leading to unknown class errors.

**Describe the bug**
```py
import sqlalchemy as sa
import sqlalchemy.orm

try:
    from sqlalchemy.orm import registry
    Base = registry().generate_base()
except ImportError:
    from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
    Base = declarative_base()

@sa.event.listens_for(sa.orm.Mapper, "after_configured")
def go1():
    print(">> mapper configured")

@sa.event.listens_for(sa.orm.Mapper, "instrument_class")
def go2(mapper, cls):
    print(">> class instrument", cls)

class Bar(Base):
    __tablename__ = "bar"
    id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
    foo_id = sa.Column(sa.ForeignKey("foo.id"))

class Foo(Base):
    __tablename__ = "foo"

    id = sa.Column(sa.Integer, primary_key=True)
    barNum = sa.orm.column_property(
        sa.select([sa.func.count(Bar.id)])
        .where(Bar.foo_id == id)
        .correlate_except(Bar)
        .as_scalar()
    )

print("class loaded. call configure_mappers()")
sa.orm.configure_mappers()
print("done")
```

**Expected behavior**
In 1.3 this gets printed:
```
>> class instrument <class '__main__.Bar'>
>> class instrument <class '__main__.Foo'>
class loaded. call configure_mappers()
>> mapper configured
done
```
in 1.4 isntead (ignoring the as_scalar warning)
```
>> class instrument <class '__main__.Bar'>
>> mapper configured
>> class instrument <class '__main__.Foo'>
class loaded. call configure_mappers()
>> mapper configured
done
```

```py
    barNum = sa.orm.column_property(
        sa.select([sa.func.count(Bar.id)])
        .where(Bar.foo_id == id)
        .correlate_except(Bar.__table__)
        .as_scalar()
    )
```

Hi,

I have come across some unexpected behaviour when using dataclasses mapped to SQLAlchemy using classical mapping.

Here's a snippet with the essence of the issue:

```python
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

from sqlalchemy import Column, Table, String, Boolean
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base
from sqlalchemy.orm import mapper, sessionmaker

Base = declarative_base()
metadata = Base.metadata

table = Table(
            "table",
            metadata,
            #
            Column("id", String, primary_key=True),
            Column("active", Boolean),
            )


@dataclass
class C:
    id: str
    active: bool = True


@dataclass
class C1:
    id: str
    active: bool


@dataclass
class C2:
    id: str
    active: bool = field(default_factory=lambda: True)


mapper(C, table)
mapper(C1, table)
mapper(C2, table)

Session = sessionmaker()
session = Session()

query = session.query(C)
print(query.filter(C.active == True))
print()

# Result (WRONG)
# SELECT "table".id AS table_id
# FROM "table"
# WHERE true

query = session.query(C1)
print(query.filter(C1.active == True))
print()

# Result: OK
# SELECT "table".id AS table_id, "table".active AS table_active
# FROM "table"
# WHERE "table".active = true

query = session.query(C2)
print(query.filter(C2.active == True))
print()

# Result: OK
# SELECT "table".id AS table_id, "table".active AS table_active
# FROM "table"
# WHERE "table".active = true
```

So, yes, I have found a workaround (using `= field(default_factory=lambda: something)` as an initializer instead of just `= something`), but it doesn't look as good.

Is there some general advice regarding the interaction of dataclasses and SQLAlchemy ORM? (I have also tried with attrs, and got the same issue).

items.title: handle DBAPI ImportErrors properly

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: engine
labels.description: engines, connections, transactions, isolation levels, execution options

items.body:
**Migrated issue, originally created by Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek))**

right now all the database modules do some combination of module-level imports, silently catching errors and setting dbapis to None, etc., this is so that all database modules are importable on all systems and dialects are creatable, even if the DBAPI is not installed in the environment.  this functionality is required for testing as well as the usage of database dialects to generate SQL independently of their target platform.

a consistent module-importing scheme should be developed which pushes all imports into a standard place and raises errors, but those errors are only reported when the DBAPI is required, i.e. when you want to create an engine with the DBAPI.

so requirements:

 * all dialects should include a "module" keyword argument, where a module can be passed to the dialect that serves as its DBAPI.
 * all database modules need some standard "module importing" method which raises ImportError as appropriate.
 * engine/strategies.py DefaultEngineStrategy needes to report these ImportErrors where it currently says "Cant get DBAPI module for dialect '%s'".
 * engine/default.py _figure_paramstyle needs to *optionally* load the DBAPI from the dialect.  no exception should be raised.  this implies that a dialect needs to attempt to load the DBAPI modules, fail, not report the error, but *do* report the error for a create_engine() call.
 * the DBAPI modules should probably be local to the Dialect, and not even be module-wide, so that the create_engine() call can repeatedly be called and will repeatedly raise ImportErrors if modules arent loadable.
 * MS-SQL is going to need some tinkering here, since it has functionality to load three different modules now.  it might be useful (or maybe not) for use_adodbapi(), use_pymssql(), etc. functions return some kind of strategy object that is used by the dialect for the functions it provides (i.e. connect, do_commit, make_connect_string) so that these functions are local.

i think this ticket is pretty high priority since the first issue new users are going to hit is that their DBAPI is not importable and this is a point of confusion.
